body.p: I. Status of the Claims

In the Non-Final Office Action dated September 10, 2024 (the "Non-Final Office Action"),1 the Examiner rejected claims 1-20 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2010/0130873 to Yuen et al. ("Yuen") in view of "Heart Rate Estimated from Body Movements at Six Degrees of Freedom by Convolutional Neural Networks" to Lee et al. ("Lee").
By this Amendment, Applicant amends claims 1-4, 8, 9, 11, and 14-20. Claims 21-42 were previously cancelled. Claims 1-20 are pending and under examination in this application.
II. Examiner Interview of October 25, 2024

Applicant's representative thanks Examiner Remaly for the courtesies extended during the Examiner Interview of October 25, 2024. During the interview, Applicant's representative discussed the rejections of independent claims 1 and 14 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 and possible amendments to the claims. No agreement was reached.
III. Rejection of Claims 1-20 under 35 U.S.C. Q 103
The Office Action rejects claims 1-20 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Yuen in view of Lee. Office Action, pp. 2-6. These rejections should be withdrawn.
A. Claim ]
Amended independent claim 1 recites a combination of elements, including, inter alia:
"a heart signal extractor configured to receive channel signals from the receive antenna elements and in response extract a heart signal using a convolutional neural network
(CNN);
a phase extractor configured to receive the channel signals and in response generate projection signals by isolating groups of the channel signals into different buckets; and

1 The Non-Final Office Action may contain statements reflecting characterizations of the related art and the claims. Regardless of whether any such statement is identified herein, Applicant declines to automatically subscribe to any statement or characterization in the Non-Final Office Action.
an extractor configured to identify a spatial beam for analyzing wireless reflections based
on the extracted heart signal and the generated projection signals"
(emphases added). None of Yuen or Lee, alone or in combination, teaches or suggest the combination of elements recited in amended independent claim 1.

Yuen discloses a "radar-based physiological motion sensor," where "Doppler-shifted signals can be extracted from the signals received by the sensor" and "[the] Doppler-shifted signals can be digitized and processed subsequently to extract information related to the cardiopulmonary motion in one or more subjects," such as "respiratory rates, heart rates, waveforms due to respiratory and cardiac activity, direction of arrival, [or] abnormal or paradoxical breathing." Yuen, Abstract.

In the Office Action, the Examiner admits that Yuen "fail[s] to explicitly teach wherein the heart signal extractor compris[es] a convolutional neural network," but relies on Lee as allegedly teaching these elements. Office Action, p. 3. Lee discloses a "study [that] aimed to develop a novel method to enhance heart rate estimation from thoracic movement by CNNs [(convolutional neural networks])." Lee, p. 1. Lee discloses measuring thoracic movement "by six-axis accelerometer and gyroscope signals using a wearable sensor that can be worn by simply clipping on clothes." Lee, p. 1. Lee discloses then using a "CNN model" to enhance heart rate estimation based on the accelerometer and gyroscope signals. Lee, p. 3.

The Examiner alleges that "[i]t would be obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the invention of Yuen et al. with the features of Lee et al. for the benefit of improving signal accuracy." Office Action, p. 3. Applicant respectfully disagrees. As admitted by the Examiner (see Office Action, p. 3), Yuen does not teach use of a CNN. And while Lee discloses a study relating to using a CNN to enhance heart rate estimation based on accelerometer and gyroscope signals, Lee does not teach or suggest using a CNN to extract a heart signal in response to "channel signals [received] from [] receive antenna elements," where the receive antenna elements are configured to "receive wireless reflections of [] transmitted wireless signals," as recited in claim 1 (emphasis added). The Examiner fails to articulate a reasoning, grounded in facts, as to why it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art to modify the system of Yuen to utilize a CNN to extract a heart signal in response to channel signals received from receive antenna elements configured to receive wireless reflections of transmitted wireless

signals based on the teachings of Lee. See USPTO Updated Guidance for Making a Proper Determination of Obviousness, Fed. Reg. Vol. 89, No. 39, 14449, 14452 (2024) ("This updated guidance reinforces the directive that Office personnel are required to provide a clear articulation of their reasoning, grounded in relevant facts, when making a determination that a claim would have been obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103"). Such a modification would not have been obvious. For at least these reasons, the rejection of independent claim 1 should be withdrawn.

Notwithstanding the above, Applicant has further amended independent claim 1 to recite "a phase extractor configured to receive the channel signals and in response generate projection signals by isolating groups of the channel signals into different buckets." None of Yuen or Lee, alone or in combination, teaches or suggests these elements. For these reasons as well, the rejection of independent claim 1 should be withdrawn.

Applicant has also amended independent claim 1 to recite "an extractor configured to identify a spatial beam for analyzing wireless reflections based on the extracted heart signal and the generated projection signals" (emphasis added). Yuen merely discloses use of its system to identify variables such as "heart rate," "heart beat-to-beat interval," and/or "heart rate variability." Yuen, [0107]; see also Yuen at [0158]-[0160], [0316], [0328]. Lee merely discloses estimating "heart rate" based on accelerometer and gyroscope signals using a CNN. Lee, p. 1. None of Yuen or Lee, alone or in combination, teaches or suggests "identify[ing] a spatial beam for analyzing wireless reflections based on the extracted heart signal and the generated projection signals" as recited in amended independent claim 1 (emphasis added). For these reasons as well, the rejection of independent claim 1 should be withdrawn.
B. Claim 2

Claim 2 depends from independent claim 1, and therefore incorporates all recitations therein. Thus, the rejection of claim 2 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should also be withdrawn for at least the reasons discussed above with respect to independent claim 1.

Claim 2 has also been amended to recite a "wireless-to-seismocardiogram translator configured to implement a machine-learning model to translate information extracted from the spatial beam to a seismocardiogram." In the Office Action, the Examiner admits that Yuen "fail[s] to explicitly teach a machine-learning model," but relies on Lee as teaching these elements. Office Action, p. 5. The Examiner alleges that "[i]t would be obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art

to modify the invention of Yuen et al. with the features of Lee et al. for the benefit of improving signal accuracy." Office Action, p. 5. Applicant respectfully disagrees for reasons similar to those discussed above with respect to claim 1. That is, as admitted by the Examiner (see Office Action, p. 5), Yuen does not teach use of a machine learning model. And while Lee discloses a study relating to using a CNN to enhance heart rate estimation based on accelerometer and gyroscope signals, Lee does not teach or suggest using a CNN to "translate information from [a] spatial beam to a seismocardiogram," as recited in claim 2 (emphasis added). The Examiner fails to articulate a reasoning, grounded in facts, as to why it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art to modify the system of Yuen to utilize a CNN to translate information from a spatial beam to a seismocardiogram based on the teachings of Lee. See USPTO Updated Guidance for Making a Proper Determination of Obviousness, Fed. Reg. Vol. 89, No. 39, 14449, 14452 (2024). Such a modification would not have been obvious. For these reasons as well, the rejection of claim 2 should be withdrawn.
C. Claim 3

Claim 3 depends from independent claim 1, and therefore incorporates all recitations therein. Thus, the rejection of claim 3 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should also be withdrawn for at least the reasons discussed above with respect to independent claim 1.

Claim 3 has also been amended to recite "an automatic labeler configured to label features of a seismocardiogram." None of Yuen or Lee, alone or in combination, teaches or suggests these additional elements of claim 3. For these reasons as well, the rejection of claim 3 should be withdrawn.
D. Claim 4

Claim 4 depends from dependent claim 3, which depends from independent claim 1. Claim 4 therefore incorporates all recitations therein. Thus, the rejection of claim 4 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should also be withdrawn for at least the reasons discussed above with respect to independent claim 1 and with respect to dependent claim 3.

Claim 4 has also been amended to recite that "the features comprise at least two features within a heart beat in the seismocardiogram." None of Yuen or Lee, alone or in combination, teaches or suggests these additional elements of claim 4. For these reasons as well, the rejection of claim 4 should be withdrawn.
E. Claims 5-11

Each of claims 5-11 depends from independent claim 1, and therefore incorporates all recitations therein. Thus, the rejections of claims 5-11 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should also be withdrawn for at least the reasons discussed above with respect to independent claim 1.
F. Claims 12 and 13

Each of claims 12 and 13 depends from independent claim 1, and therefore incorporates all recitations therein. Thus, the rejections of claims 12 and 13 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should also be withdrawn for at least the reasons discussed above with respect to independent claim 1.

In the Office Action, the Examiner also cites paragraphs [0170], [0273], [0280], and [0348]-[0350] of Yuen as allegedly teaching operation in the "acoustic frequency range" (claim 12) and in the "ultrasonic frequency range" (claim 13). Office Action, p. 5. Applicant respectfully disagrees. None of paragraphs [0170], [0273], [0280], or [0348]-[0350], or any other portion of Yuen, discusses operation in an "acoustic frequency range" (claim 12) or in an "ultrasonic frequency range" (claim 13). For these additional reasons, the rejections of claims 12 and 13 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should be withdrawn.
G. Claim 14
Amended independent claim 14 recites a combination of elements, including, inter alia:
"at least one processor configured to:
translate [] wireless signals to a seismocardiogram based on coefficients
determined using a first machine learning model; and
detect and label at least two features in at least one heart beat in the
seismocardiogram using a second, different, machine learning model"
(emphases added). None of Yuen or Lee, alone or in combination, teaches or suggests the combination of elements recited in amended independent claim 14.

In the Office Action, the Examiner admits that Yuen "fail[s] to explicitly teach a machine- learning model," but relies on Lee as allegedly teaching these elements. Office Action, p. 5. The Examiner alleges that "[i]t would be obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the invention of Yuen et al. with the features of Lee et al. for the benefit of improving the signal accuracy." Office Action, p. 5. Applicant respectfully disagrees. As admitted by the Examiner

(see Office Action, p. 5), Yuen does not teach use of a machine learning model. And while Lee discloses a study relating to using a CNN to enhance heart rate estimation based on accelerometer and gyroscope signals, Lee does not teach or suggest using a CNN, let alone coefficients determined using a first machine learning model, to translate wireless signals to a seismocardiogram, as recited in amended independent claim 14 (emphasis added). The Examiner fails to articulate a reasoning, grounded in facts, as to why it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art to modify Yuen to utilize a CNN to translate wireless signals to a seismocardiogram based on the teachings of Lee. See USPTO Updated Guidance for Making a Proper Determination of Obviousness, Fed. Reg. Vol. 89, No. 39, 14449, 14452 (2024). Such a modification would not have been obvious. For at least these reasons, the rejection of claim 14 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should be withdrawn.

Independent claim 14 has further been amended to recite that the at least one processor is configured to "detect and label at least two features in at least one heart beat in the seismocardiogram using a second, different, machine learning model" (emphases added). None of Yuen or Lee, alone or in combination, teaches or suggests detecting and labeling at least two features in at least one heart beat in a seismocardiogram, let alone doing so using a second, different machine learning model. For these reasons as well, the rejection of independent claim 14 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should be withdrawn.
H. Claims 1 Sand 16

Each of claims 15 and 16 depends from independent claim 14, and therefore incorporates all recitations therein. Thus, the rejections of claims 15 and 16 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should also be withdrawn for at least the reasons discussed above with respect to independent claim 14.
I. Claim 17

Claim 17 depends from independent claim 14, and therefore incorporates all recitations therein. Thus, the rejection of claim 17 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should also be withdrawn for at least the reasons discussed above with respect to independent claim 14.
Claim 17 has been further amended to recite that the "at least two features comprises five features, the five features corresponding to an aortic valve opening (AO), aortic valve closing
(AC), mitral valve opening (MO), mitral valve closing (MC), and isovolumetric contracting (IM)."
None of Yuen or Lee, alone or in combination, teaches or suggests these additional elements. For these reasons as well, the rejection of claim 17 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should be withdrawn.
J. Claim 18

Claim 18 depends from independent claim 14, and therefore incorporates all recitations therein. Thus, the rejection of claim 18 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should also be withdrawn for at least the reasons discussed above with respect to independent claim 14.
K. Claims 19 and 20

Claims 19 and 20 depend from independent claim 14, and therefore incorporate all recitations therein. Thus, the rejections of claims 19 and 20 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should also be withdrawn for at least the reasons discussed above with respect to independent claim 14.

In the Office Action, the Examiner also cites paragraphs [0170], [0273], [0280], and [0348]-[0350] of Yuen as allegedly teaching that the "receiver is configured to receive acoustic signals" (claim 19) and that the "receiver is configured to receive ultrasonic frequency signals" (claim 20). Office Action, p. 6. Applicant respectfully disagrees. None of paragraphs [0170], [0273], [0280], or [0348]-[0350], or any other portion of Yuen, discusses receiving "acoustic signals" (claim 19) or "ultrasonic signals" (claim 20). For these additional reasons, the rejections of claims 19 and 20 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should be withdrawn.
TV. Conclusion
In view of the above, Applicant believes the present application is in condition for allowance, for which a notice thereof is respectfully requested.
The Examiner is respectfully invited to telephone the undersigned if there are any questions regarding this Amendment or this application.

It is believed that all the pending claims have been addressed. However, the absence of a reply to a specific rejection, issue or comment does not signify agreement with or concession of that rejection, issue or comment. In addition, because the arguments made above may not be exhaustive, there may be reasons for withdrawing the prior art cited with regards to any or all pending claims (or other claims) that have not been expressed. Finally, nothing in this paper should be construed as intent to concede any issue with regard to any claim, except as specifically
stated in this paper, and the amendment of any claim does not necessarily signify concession of unpatentability of the claim prior to its amendment.

The Commissioner is hereby authorized to charge payment of any additional fees associated with this communication or credit any overpayment to Deposit Account No. 500845, including, but not limited to, any charges for extensions of time under 37 C.F.R. § 1.136.
Respectfully submitted,
Dated: December 10, 2024 DALY, CROWLEY, MOFFORD & DURKEE, LLP
